logline: Oz Cobb - the Penguin - claws his way from foot soldier to Gotham crime boss in the power vacuum left after the events of The Batman, dismantling everything in his path.

renewal.note: A limited series of eight episodes; no second season announced as of June 2026.

bollymeter.basis: 95% on Rotten Tomatoes from 195 critics. Colin Farrell's transformation and Cristin Milioti's scene-stealing Sofia Falcone gave critics what amounted to a character study wrapped in a mob drama - darker and more precise than superhero TV typically manages.

pull_quotes.text: A ferociously entertaining crime drama elevated by two powerhouse lead performances - and Colin Farrell is unrecognisable in the best possible way.

seasons.review_body: The Penguin is the best argument DC has made in years for the superhero-adjacent limited series format. Lauren LeFranc built eight episodes around Oz Cobb's ascent - and crucially, the show works as a crime drama first and a DC property second. Colin Farrell under three hours of prosthetics delivers a performance of genuine menace and dark comedy, but the critical surprise was Cristin Milioti as Sofia Falcone: wounded, brilliant, and terrifying. Critics pointed to the show's willingness to let Gotham be genuinely grimy - no CGI spectacle, mostly intimate rooms and bad decisions. The 5.3 million viewers at launch were the highest-rated HBO premiere in two years, and the critical score (95% RT) put it among the best DC productions ever made.

episode_reviews.title: After Hours
episode_reviews.spoiler_free: The Penguin picks up immediately after the Riddler's flooding of Gotham in The Batman (2022), dropping Oz Cobb into the power vacuum with nothing but audacity and tactical instinct. The premiere establishes the series' register - Sopranos-adjacent mob drama with superhero-adjacent origin story - and confirms that Colin Farrell's prosthetic transformation is matched by a performance of comparable depth.
episode_reviews.the_moment: Oz Cobb surveying a flooded, ruined Gotham and calculating exactly how to turn catastrophe into opportunity - the moment that defines the character for the entire run.
episode_reviews.review_body: The Penguin's premiere operates as a thesis statement: this is not a superhero series but a crime drama that happens to occupy a superhero-adjacent world. Set in the immediate aftermath of The Batman's Riddler flooding Gotham, the episode drops Oz Cobb into a power vacuum and watches him work. Colin Farrell's physical transformation via prosthetics is extraordinary, but the performance underneath it is the real achievement - Oz is calculating, resentful, and genuinely funny in ways that make him compelling even at his most brutal. At 95% on Rotten Tomatoes from 195 critics, the series earned that response largely from how the premiere established its tonal commitment. The decision to frame a Batman universe spinoff as a Sopranos-inflected character study proved immediately effective in the opening episode.

episode_reviews.title: Sofia in Wonderland
episode_reviews.spoiler_free: Episode 3 is The Penguin's formal statement of ambition: a Sofia Falcone backstory episode that operates as a standalone psychological portrait. Cristin Milioti's performance is the episode's whole argument - what happens to a woman whose patrician family processes her as a liability. The episode reframes the entire season.
episode_reviews.the_moment: Sofia's account of Arkham - the specific, calm way she describes what happened to her there - the scene that makes the entire season's power dynamic suddenly legible.
episode_reviews.review_body: Episode 3 is where The Penguin earns the ambition its premise promised. A backstory episode focused entirely on Sofia Falcone, it operates as a standalone psychological portrait of what happens to a woman when a powerful family processes her as a liability and a secret. Cristin Milioti's performance is the hour's whole argument - Sofia's calm, precise account of what Arkham cost her reframes the entire season's power dynamics in a single scene. The decision to give Sofia a full episode this early demonstrates that the series is genuinely interested in a co-protagonist structure rather than positioning Oz as the unchallenged centre. The 95% RT score reflects a series that earned its reception through formal choices like this one.

episode_reviews.title: A Great or Little Thing
episode_reviews.spoiler_free: The Penguin's finale resolves the mob war it has been building since the premiere and delivers on Oz Cobb's coronation as the series' title character in both name and power. A satisfying close that earns its darkness without exploiting it, and leaves Gotham's gangland in a configuration the broader DC universe will have to reckon with.
episode_reviews.the_moment: Oz's final act against the Falcone family - the specific, precise nature of his vengeance, which makes his transformation into the Penguin feel inevitable rather than scripted.
episode_reviews.review_body: The finale of The Penguin delivers on the mob drama the series established in episode 1. Oz Cobb's arc from opportunistic lieutenant to crime lord completes itself here with a specificity the DC universe rarely achieves in its origin stories. The violence of the climax is earned rather than spectacular - the series has done the character work to make the Penguin's emergence feel inevitable. Sofia Falcone's arc reaches its conclusion in a way that maintains the co-protagonist structure that distinguished the series from a straightforward villain spinoff. At 95% RT and 8.2 IMDb, the finale contributes to a limited series that holds up as DC's best-executed character study in the streaming era.
